CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5 · 22 HABITAT LESSONS

Animals & Their Habitats.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Twenty-two animals, twenty-two right homes.

Every animal in this class has its own step-by-step lesson: open the card together, find the animal and its home, say the habitat word, follow the teaching steps, ask the questions and finish with a game that puts your child inside that home — hopping the grassland, huddling like penguins, hanging like a bat. The order is gentle: homes near home first — the meadow and the pond — then the forests, the warm grasslands and the desert, the fresh and salt water, the freezing poles, and finally the dark cave.

One card a sitting is plenty; the whole class is a month of five-minute animal visits. By the end, the big question of early science — where does this animal live, and why THERE? — has twenty-two answered examples, from a rabbit in the tall grass to a whale in the deep blue.

A HOME FOR EVERY ANIMAL

Matching animals to their addresses.

Habitats are the first matching game in science: every animal carries its home in its body. The camel carries the desert in its feet and lashes, the polar bear wears the arctic as camouflage, the koala holds one tree in its tummy and its arms. Once your child can ask "could the whale live in the desert?" — and laugh at the answer — the whole set has done its work.

The cards love to be sorted. Lay them out and make home-piles: grass homes, tree homes, water homes, ice homes, the cave. Every sort is a different lesson, and no two children sort them quite the same way — all of them are right.

AFTER THE HABITAT LESSONS

Then meet the dinosaurs.

Class 36 sorts the animals of today by where they live; the school’s Dinosaurs extra class adds the ancient cast with thirty-three cards a child can move to — stomp like a T. rex, make three pretend horns, glide like a giant flyer. Every card prints its own activity, every dinosaur has a lesson and a printable card, and the deck opens with the six favorites. When today’s habitat lesson ends, let the Cretaceous take the last five minutes.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 22 cards in Animals & Their Habitats, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Animals & Their Habitats. We have 22 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Rabbit

    “The rabbit lives in the meadow. Tall grass to nibble, tall grass to hide in.”

    How: On a grassy patch or a park lawn, crouch down to rabbit height and look around. From down there the grass is a forest — that is exactly how a meadow feels to a rabbit.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Frog

    “The frog lives at the pond. It sits on the pad by day and plops into the water when anyone comes near.”

    How: Visit any pond, even a small one, and play pond-spotter: listen for croaks, look for ripples, scan the lily pads. One real "I heard one!" beats ten pictures.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Squirrel

    “The squirrel lives in the woodland. It gathers nuts all autumn and hides them for the cold days.”

    How: Hide five "acorns" (any small objects) around a room and let your child be the squirrel, gathering them into one stash. Ask afterwards: can they remember where all five went?

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Fox

    “The fox lives at the edge of the woodland. It sleeps by day and goes trotting when the sun goes down.”

    How: Play fox-following on an evening walk or in a corridor game: quiet feet, light steps, weaving between obstacles. Foxes are famous for moving without a sound.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Owl

    “The owl lives up in the forest trees. Big eyes for seeing in the dark, soft wings for flying without a sound.”

    How: Wait for dusk, open a window and listen for one full minute. Owls call most at twilight — and even in a town, an owl’s hoot is a real possibility.

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Koala

    “The koala lives in the eucalyptus forest. It eats the leaves and sleeps in the branches, nearly all day long.”

    How: Do the koala hug: arms around a doorframe or a grown-up’s leg, hold on for a slow count of ten. Koalas grip like that for hours — stronger fingers than they look.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Panda

    “The panda lives in the bamboo forest. Its favourite food — breakfast, lunch and dinner — is bamboo.”

    How: Snap a crisp breadstick or a raw carrot into "bamboo" pieces and let your child munch sitting cross-legged like a panda, holding the stalk in both front paws.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Monkey

    “The monkey lives in the rainforest, up in the treetops. Vines and branches are its roads.”

    How: Play the rainforest game at a playground climbing frame: cross without touching the ground, hand over hand like a monkey. The floor is the forest floor — nobody lives down there.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Zebra

    “The zebra lives on the grassland, where the grass grows tall enough to hide in but the sky goes on forever.”

    How: Do the stripe test with a striped sock or ribbon: wave it among plain things and count how hard it is to say exactly where one stripe ends. A moving dazzle of stripes confuses eyes.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Kangaroo

    “The kangaroo lives on the grassland. It cannot walk backwards — it hops, and hopping is faster anyway.”

    How: Kangaroo-hop races across the lawn or the hallway: feet together, hands as little paws. Ten hops is a proper kangaroo distance.

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Elephant

    “The elephant lives on the savanna. It knocks down trees, digs for water and walks miles — and the whole savanna follows.”

    How: Elephant-water-hole dig: in a sandpit or a bowl of dry oats, dig with one "trunk" arm until you hit the hidden "water" (a cup or a blue cloth buried underneath).

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Lion

    “The lion lives on the savanna. It rests in the shade for most of the day and does its busy work when it is cooler.”

    How: Play pride-nap, then prowl: everyone lies down together for a slow lion count of twenty, then rises, stretches and prowls one slow circle around the room. Only the prowl earns the nap.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · Camel

    “The camel lives in the desert. Its hump is not water — it stores fat for the long walk between oases.”

    How: Balance test, camel-style: walk heel-to-toe across a "dune" of cushions or a line of tape. Wide, steady feet keep you on top of soft sand — camels have the original all-terrain soles.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · Beaver

    “The beaver lives by the river. It builds dams from sticks and mud until the water makes a pond — its very own house address.”

    How: Build a mini dam: in a tray or at the bath, stack twigs, spoons or blocks across the trickle and watch the water pool behind it. Your child has done what beavers do.

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Turtle

    “The turtle lives at the coast. It swims in the sea all day and comes ashore to rest on the warm sand.”

    How: Two-home game: one side of the room is "sea", the other is "beach". Call out turtle actions — swim, bask, lay eggs, dive — and let your child dash between the two homes.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · Fish

    “The fish lives in the ocean. It cannot breathe air like us — it breathes the water itself, through its gills.”

    How: Gill-breathing pantomime: open and close your mouth like a fish and whisper "we breathe water, fish breathe air — we could never swap!" Then count how many fish-shaped things are in the bath tonight.

  20. 18
    Card 17 · Dolphin

    “The dolphin lives in the ocean and comes up to breathe. It talks to its family in clicks and whistles.”

    How: Dolphin up-breath game: swim-crawl along the carpet, then "surface" every few strokes with a big loud breath. Dolphins plan their hops exactly like that.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · Whale

    “The whale lives in the ocean. It is bigger than a bus, and its babies are bigger than your dad.”

    How: Whale-size walk: pace out a bus-length on the pavement or the corridor, heel to toe. The whole family standing nose-to-tail fits inside one whale — that is the point.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · Penguin

    “The penguin lives in the polar region, where the sea is ice. It is a bird that swims instead of flying.”

    How: Waddle-and-slide: penguin-walk across the room, then belly-slide the last stretch onto a cushion "ice floe". Real penguins travel exactly this way.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Seal

    “The seal lives in the polar region. It flops out onto the ice to rest and slips into the sea to hunt.”

    How: Seal move challenge: from lying flat, push up onto hands and toes and scoot forward three "floppers". Harder than it looks — seals make it look easy.

  24. Cards 21–22
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Polar Bear

    “The polar bear lives in the arctic, on the ice above the deep cold sea. Its fur matches the snow so well it can vanish.”

    How: Camouflage test: hold a white paper polar bear cut-out against a white wall, then against a colourful poster. Which one is hard to see? That is the whole arctic trick.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · Bat

    “The bat lives in the cave and hangs upside down by its feet. At night it flies out to hunt; by day the cave is its bedroom.”

    How: Hang like a bat: drape your child face-down over a grown-up’s arm, head lower than heels, for a five-count of bat-hang. Then flap once, twice, and "fly" back upright.

  27. 24
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  28. 25
    Check

    “Can you find Rabbit? Now show me Lion.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  29. 26
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 22 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Desert Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle the desert survivors, match them to dunes, rocks and burrows, count the cacti and trace the word DESERT.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then circle, match, count, choose and trace straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/animals-and-their-habitatsdesert-animals-and-their-habitat/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The desert is hot and dry, and the animals that live there are built for it — padded feet, big ears, burrows under the sand.

Knowledge to have ready: The word desert, and three desert residents your child can name on sight: camel, fennec fox and lizard.

Why this activity matters: Saying who does NOT belong is the fast route to understanding who does — the penguin and the bear make the desert definition sharp.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Matching animals to homes
  • Counting to 4
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: The desert is the hottest, driest home on the sheet — let us find the animals who can take the heat.

What to look for on the sheet: For the fennec fox ears — huge ears are desert air-conditioning, and your child will love knowing why.

Questions to ask along the way: Could the penguin live here? Why not? What would the camel say about all that ice?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Start with the camel — everyone knows that one — and let the other two circle themselves around it.

Parent tips: Sand in a tray plus a toy camel turns the matching row into a small world after the sheet is done.

Understanding check: Name one animal from the sheet that would hate the desert — and say why in your own words.

Real-life practice: On a hot sunny walk, ask: who is the camel of our neighborhood today?

This activity belongs to Class 36 — Animals & Their Habitats on the Learning Path. Progress is saved on this device for the child chosen in My Classroom — and only a real save of finished work marks it cleared, never just opening the page.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Farm Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle the farm team, match cow, pig, hen and sheep to their homes, count the hay bales and trace FARM.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/animals-and-their-habitatsfarm-animals-and-their-habitat/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: A farm is a habitat people built: every animal on it has a home with a name — barn, sty, coop, pen.

Knowledge to have ready: The farm team — cow, horse, pig, hen and sheep — and the word farm for the place they all live.

Why this activity matters: The farm is usually a child's first habitat with names for the homes themselves, which plants the idea that where you live has a word.

  • Farm animal names
  • Home vocabulary: barn, sty, coop, pen
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: The farm is the one habitat with a barn in it. Let us get every animal home before supper.

What to look for on the sheet: For the lion sitting in the circle row — he does not belong, and catching him is the game.

Questions to ask along the way: Who sleeps in the barn? Who loves the mud? Which animal on this sheet have you seen for real?

Helpful hints without giving it away: The sheep is not in the circle row — she appears in the matching row, so keep her home ready too.

Parent tips: After the sheet, line up toy farm animals and build each home from blocks — the words come out on their own.

Understanding check: Ask where the pig lives, where the hen lives — two answers, no paper, real memory.

Real-life practice: Visit a farm or a petting zoo and find one home from the sheet in real life — barns count double.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Forest Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle the forest dwellers, match them to hollows, dens and thickets, count the trees and trace FOREST.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/animals-and-their-habitatsforest-animals-and-their-habitat/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The forest is a home you can walk under: tall trees give food, shade and hiding places, and every forest animal uses them its own way.

Knowledge to have ready: The word forest, and three forest neighbors — squirrel, bear and deer — plus the fox who lives there too.

Why this activity matters: Forests are the habitat children meet in storybooks first; naming its residents turns familiar pictures into real knowledge.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Matching animals to homes
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: Under the tall trees lives a whole neighborhood — let us meet who hides in the forest.

What to look for on the sheet: For the camel standing in the circle row — sand feet have no business in the woods, and that is the laugh of the sheet.

Questions to ask along the way: Who stores food in a tree? Who sleeps all winter? Where would you hide if you were small and furry?

Helpful hints without giving it away: The tree hollow and the bush are close together in the matching row — slow lines, no guessing.

Parent tips: On the next walk under trees, play spot-the-home: holes, nests, burrows all count.

Understanding check: Point at the deer: what does the forest give it to eat? Leaves and twigs is a right answer.

Real-life practice: Collect one fallen leaf on your next walk and call it forest mail — delivered to the fridge.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Ocean Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle who lives under the waves, match whale, clownfish and turtle to their ocean homes, count fish and trace OCEAN.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/animals-and-their-habitatsocean-animals-and-their-habitat/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The ocean is the biggest habitat on Earth — and even inside it, animals split it up: the reef, the open water, the sandy floor.

Knowledge to have ready: The word ocean, and three ocean residents on the sheet: whale, clownfish and sea turtle.

Why this activity matters: Splitting one huge habitat into addresses — reef, open sea, seabed — is the first step from "fish live in water" to real ecology.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Matching animals to ocean homes
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 6
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: The ocean is one home so big it has rooms inside it — let us find who lives where.

What to look for on the sheet: For the cow standing quietly in the circle row — dry land is her whole world, and that is the point.

Questions to ask along the way: Who breathes air but lives in the sea? (The whale — a real surprise.) Who paints the reef orange?

Helpful hints without giving it away: The seabed scene has seaweed on the sand — that clue separates it from the open blue water.

Parent tips: A bathtub becomes the open sea, a sponge the reef — retell the matching row with bath toys.

Understanding check: Name two animals from the sheet that could never live in the ocean — and one that could.

Real-life practice: At bath time or a aquarium visit, use the three ocean words: reef, open sea, seabed.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Polar Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle who thrives in the ice, match polar bear, penguin and arctic fox to their icy homes, count ice blocks and trace POLAR.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/animals-and-their-habitatspolar-animals-and-their-habitat/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The polar regions are the coldest habitats on Earth, and their animals wear built-in coats — thick fur or a layer of fat.

Knowledge to have ready: The word polar, and three ice-ready residents: polar bear, penguin and arctic fox.

Why this activity matters: Extreme habitats make the matching rule obvious: nobody survives the ice without the right equipment, and the sheet shows exactly whose bodies have it.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Matching animals to icy homes
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: The coldest homes on Earth belong to the warmest-dressed animals — let us meet the polar team.

What to look for on the sheet: For the monkey in the circle row — jungle arms would freeze in a minute, and your child will know exactly why.

Questions to ask along the way: What do polar bears and penguins both wear that we have to zip on? Who slides on their tummy?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Flat floating ice is the floe, tall pointy ice is the icebergs — say the two words and the match does itself.

Parent tips: Freeze a small bowl of water, slide the toy penguin on top, and the floe word becomes real.

Understanding check: Ask which is colder, our winter or the polar regions — then ask what the fox wears to be sure.

Real-life practice: Next snowy or cold day, one minute of penguin walking — wings in, tiny steps, the word polar said twice.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Wetland Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle who lives in the wetland, match frog, egret and crocodile to their soggy homes, count lily pads and trace WETLAND.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/animals-and-their-habitatswetland-animals-and-their-habitat/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: A wetland is land that is soaked — ponds, reeds and mud — and it is a dinner, a bath and a hiding place all at once.

Knowledge to have ready: The word wetland, and three wetland regulars on the sheet: frog, egret and crocodile.

Why this activity matters: The wetland is the habitat that is neither dry nor deep — naming it teaches children that habitats come in every in-between flavor, not just desert versus ocean.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Matching animals to wetland homes
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 4
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: Where the water meets the grass, the wetland squelches — let us find who loves it that way.

What to look for on the sheet: For the duck — she is in the circle row but not the matching row, so she needs a circle and a wave goodbye.

Questions to ask along the way: Who hops and who wades? What does the crocodile use the mud for? Have you ever heard frogs at night?

Helpful hints without giving it away: The frog is the easy anchor — he lives half in the water and half on the lily pads.

Parent tips: After the sheet, jump like a frog, wade slowly like an egret and snap like a crocodile — three animals, three moves.

Understanding check: Name the three wetland homes without the paper: pond, reeds, burrow.

Real-life practice: Pass any pond or canal on your walks and ask: who from our sheet could live here?
